q: Where can I find a pharmacy near the Old Quarter in Hanoi?
check: Names one or more real pharmacies (nhà thuốc) in or near Hoan Kiem / the Old Quarter of Hanoi with a street or area, taken from map data; must not invent names or addresses, and should say so plainly if it has no map data for the area.

q: Which hospitals in Nairobi have an emergency department a foreign visitor could go to?
check: Names real Nairobi hospitals with their area, for example Aga Khan University Hospital (Parklands), The Nairobi Hospital (Upper Hill) or Kenyatta National Hospital; must not invent hospitals, and should not place them in another city.

q: vegetarian restaurants in Lima, ideally around Miraflores
check: Lists real vegetarian or vegan restaurants in Lima (Miraflores or nearby Barranco/San Isidro preferred) with street or district; must not invent names, and should admit it if it has no listings rather than guess.

q: I have an afternoon free in Vienna. Which traditional coffee houses are in the city centre?
check: Names real Viennese coffee houses in or near the Innere Stadt, such as Café Central, Café Hawelka, Demel, Café Landtmann or Café Sperl, with a rough location; no invented places.

q: Is there an English-language bookshop in Montreal I can walk to from downtown?
check: Names real Montreal bookshops selling English books with their area, for example Paragraphe or Indigo downtown, The Word near McGill, or Drawn & Quarterly in Mile End; no invented shops.

q: Where can I get halal food in Melbourne?
check: Names real halal restaurants or the areas known for them in Melbourne (for example the CBD, or Sydney Road in Brunswick/Coburg) with street or suburb; must not invent restaurants or claim halal status without a source.

q: Looking for a cheap hostel in Marrakesh close to Jemaa el-Fnaa square.
check: Names real hostels or budget riads in the Marrakesh medina within walking distance of Jemaa el-Fnaa, with a street or neighbourhood; does not quote live prices as fact and does not invent names.

q: Where are the ATMs or banks in Thamel, Kathmandu, that I can use with a foreign card?
check: Points to real banks or ATMs in or beside Thamel, Kathmandu (for example Nabil Bank, Himalayan Bank or Standard Chartered branches/ATMs) with a street or landmark; no invented locations.

q: How does my phone's GPS work out where I am when I have no mobile signal?
check: The receiver only listens to satellites: each broadcasts its position and a precise atomic-clock time, the phone measures signal travel time to get distances, and with at least four satellites solves for position and its own clock error (trilateration). No mobile network or internet is needed.

q: How do mRNA vaccines work?
check: mRNA wrapped in lipid nanoparticles enters cells, which read it to make a harmless piece of the pathogen (e.g. the spike protein); the immune system responds with antibodies and memory cells. The mRNA is short-lived, does not enter the nucleus or alter DNA.

q: How do noise-cancelling headphones actually cancel sound?
check: Microphones pick up ambient sound and the electronics play an inverted (anti-phase) copy so the two waves cancel by destructive interference; works best on steady low-frequency noise such as engine drone, less well on sudden or high-pitched sounds, which rely on passive isolation.

q: What is the difference between a virus and a bacterium, and why don't antibiotics work on a cold?
check: Bacteria are single-celled living organisms that reproduce on their own; viruses are much smaller, not cells, and can only replicate inside host cells. Antibiotics target bacterial structures (cell wall, ribosomes) that viruses lack, and colds are caused by viruses.

q: Nuclear fission vs fusion: what is the difference?
check: Fission splits heavy nuclei (uranium, plutonium) and powers today's reactors; fusion joins light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) as in the Sun, needs extreme temperature and pressure, and is not yet a commercial power source. Both release energy from the mass difference (binding energy); fusion produces less long-lived waste.

q: What's the difference between an SSD and a hard disk drive?
check: An HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters read by a moving head; an SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts. SSDs are much faster (especially random access), quieter and more shock-resistant, but cost more per gigabyte and have a limited number of write cycles.

q: Why do my ears pop when the plane is descending?
check: Cabin pressure rises on descent, so air pressure outside the eardrum exceeds that in the middle ear; the Eustachian tube must open to equalise and the pop is that equalisation. Swallowing, yawning or the Valsalva manoeuvre help; a cold can block the tube and cause pain.

q: Why are there two high tides a day when the Moon only passes overhead once?
check: The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the Earth and more weakly on the far side than on the centre, giving two bulges (tidal force is a difference in gravity); the Earth rotates through both, so high tides come about 12 h 25 min apart. The Sun adds spring and neap tides.

q: What etiquette should I know before visiting Japan for the first time?
check: Should cover several of: remove shoes indoors and in some restaurants/temples, no tipping, bow as greeting, do not stick chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick to chopstick, be quiet on trains and avoid phone calls there, wash before entering an onsen bath.

q: What plug and voltage does Switzerland use? Will my normal European two-pin plug fit?
check: Switzerland uses type J sockets (three round pins) at 230 V, 50 Hz. The slim two-pin Europlug (type C) fits, but the larger round Schuko (type F) plug generally does not fit without an adapter.

q: What number do I call in an emergency in India?
check: 112 is the single national emergency number; the older numbers still work: 100 police, 101 fire, 102 or 108 ambulance.

q: Is it safe to drink the tap water in Iceland?
check: Yes, cold tap water in Iceland is safe and of very high quality, so bottled water is unnecessary. The hot tap water is often geothermal and smells of sulphur; it is harmless but one should drink from the cold tap.

q: How much am I expected to tip at a sit-down restaurant in the United States?
check: Around 15 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill is the norm for table service (often more for very good service), because servers' wages depend on tips; about a dollar or two per drink at a bar; check whether a service charge was already added for large groups.

q: What are the ways to get from Heathrow Airport into central London by public transport?
check: Should name the Underground Piccadilly line (cheapest, roughly 50 minutes), the Elizabeth line, and the Heathrow Express to Paddington (about 15 minutes, most expensive); coaches or buses are a further option. Must not state live fares as fact.

q: What currency is used in Morocco, and can I rely on paying by card?
check: The Moroccan dirham (MAD), a closed currency that is hard to obtain outside Morocco and restricted for import/export, so exchange on arrival or use ATMs. Cards work in larger hotels, restaurants and shops in cities, but cash is needed for souks, taxis, small shops and rural areas.

q: Which side of the road do they drive on in Ireland, and are the speed limits in miles or kilometres?
check: Ireland drives on the left, with right-hand-drive cars. Speed limits in the Republic of Ireland are in km/h; Northern Ireland (part of the UK) uses mph.

q: My friend was stung by a bee and now her lips are swelling and she is wheezing. We are an hour from the nearest road. What do I do?
check: Recognise anaphylaxis: give an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector into the outer thigh at once if available, call for emergency help, lay her down with legs raised (or sitting up if breathing is hard), and repeat adrenaline after about 5 minutes if no improvement. Antihistamines are not a substitute; scrape the stinger out.

q: How do I tell heat stroke from heat exhaustion, and what should I do for heat stroke on a trail?
check: Heat stroke: core temperature about 40 C or more with confusion, collapse or seizures (skin may be hot and dry or still sweating); it is life-threatening. Call for help and cool immediately: shade, remove clothing, cold-water immersion or wet the skin and fan, ice packs at neck, armpits and groin; no drinks if not fully alert. Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, headache, clear mind; rest, cool and rehydrate.

q: An adult at our campsite is choking on food and can't speak or cough. What are the steps?
check: Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich), alternating until the object clears; call emergency services; if the person becomes unconscious, start CPR. Do not interfere if they can still cough effectively.

q: What is the right first aid for a jellyfish sting at a beach with no lifeguard?
check: Get out of the water, rinse with seawater (not fresh water), remove tentacles with tweezers or a gloved hand without rubbing, and soak in hot water (about 45 C, as hot as tolerable) for 20 minutes or more for pain. Vinegar is used for box jellyfish stings in tropical waters. Do not use urine; seek urgent help for breathing difficulty, chest pain or a large sting.

q: We're at 3,800 m on day two of a trek and I have a pounding headache and feel sick. Is that altitude sickness and should we keep going up?
check: These are typical signs of acute mountain sickness: do not ascend further, rest at the same altitude, drink, take a simple painkiller, and descend if symptoms worsen or do not improve in about a day. Loss of balance, confusion, or breathlessness at rest and a wet cough suggest cerebral or pulmonary oedema and mean descend immediately. Acetazolamide may be mentioned.

q: Caught on an exposed ridge with a thunderstorm coming in. How do we reduce the risk of being hit by lightning?
check: Get off the ridge or summit and down to lower ground quickly; avoid isolated trees, water, cave mouths and metal objects such as poles and fences; spread the group out; if caught in the open, crouch low on the balls of the feet with feet together (ideally on a pack or mat) and do not lie flat. A tent gives no protection; a closed vehicle or building does.

q: My flight leaves Auckland (UTC+12) at 19:30 on Friday and takes 12 hours 10 minutes to Los Angeles (UTC-7). What local day and time do I land?
check: 12:40 on Friday, Los Angeles time. Working: 19:30 Fri at UTC+12 = 07:30 Fri UTC; plus 12 h 10 min = 19:40 Fri UTC; minus 7 h = 12:40 Fri (earlier on the clock than the departure because of the date line).

q: My rental EV has a 60 kWh battery charged to 80% and uses 16 kWh per 100 km. If I want to arrive with 10% left, how far can I drive?
check: 262.5 km (about 260 km). Working: usable energy = 80% - 10% = 70% of 60 kWh = 42 kWh; 42 / 16 x 100 = 262.5 km.

I'm cycling 72 km tomorrow: the first 45 km at about 18 km/h, the remaining hilly part at 12 km/h, plus a 40-minute lunch stop. If I leave at 08:30, when do I arrive?
check: 13:55. Working: 45 / 18 = 2 h 30 min; remaining 27 km / 12 = 2 h 15 min; riding 4 h 45 min + 40 min stop = 5 h 25 min; 08:30 + 5:25 = 13:55.

q: My suitcase weighs 56 lb on the hotel scale and the airline limit is 23 kg. How many kilograms over am I?
check: About 2.4 kg over. Working: 56 lb x 0.4536 = 25.40 kg; 25.40 - 23 = 2.40 kg (roughly 5.3 lb to remove).

q: I can fly into either La Paz or Quito to start a South America trip. Which one is more likely to give me altitude sickness on arrival, and why?
check: La Paz: the city is at roughly 3,600 m and its airport at El Alto is about 4,000 m, whereas Quito is about 2,850 m. Altitude sickness risk rises markedly above roughly 2,500 to 3,000 m, so La Paz is the riskier arrival; advise resting and acclimatising, or starting in Quito.

q: What should I pack for a week in Leh, Ladakh in July, given how high and dry it is?
check: Must combine the facts that Leh is at about 3,500 m in a high-altitude cold desert in the Himalayan rain shadow: warm sunny days but cold nights, very strong UV, little rain. So: layers including a warm jacket, sun hat, sunglasses and high-SPF sunscreen, lip balm and moisturiser, water bottle, and plan one to two rest days to acclimatise (altitude medication may be mentioned).

q: For a trip in late December, would I get more daylight in Tromsø or in Edinburgh, and roughly how much in each?
check: Edinburgh. Tromsø (about 69.6 N) lies north of the Arctic Circle and is in polar night in late December, so the sun does not rise at all (only a few hours of midday twilight); Edinburgh (about 56 N) gets roughly 7 hours of daylight.

q: We'll be camping at 4,500 m. Will pasta take longer to cook up there, and is boiling still enough to make stream water safe to drink?
check: Air pressure is lower at altitude so water boils at about 85 C at 4,500 m (roughly 1 C lower per 300 m), which means food cooks noticeably slower. Boiling still disinfects water because pathogens are killed well below that temperature, but boil longer: about 3 minutes rather than 1 above roughly 2,000 m.
